phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b] plus short open-mid front [ɛ] — the crisp 'bed' of English, with the stress falling here as Welsh stress nearly always falls on the penult.
Voiced dental stop [d] followed by Welsh w, a full vowel here: short close back [ʊ], the 'oo' of 'book' — never the consonant 'w' of English.
Welsh final-syllable y, the close central vowel [ɨ] (southern dialects relax it toward [ɪ]), closed by a tapped or trilled [r] — the syllable that gives the name its un-English ending.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BED-weer' — stress the first syllable; read the w as the vowel 'oo' and the final y as a vowel between 'i' and 'u', with the r lightly rolled.

kin.label: Middle Welsh
kin.form: Bedwyr fab Bedrawc, 'Bedwyr son of Bedrawc' — the standard spelling of the White Book of Rhydderch and Red Book of Hergest texts

kin.label: Medieval Latin
kin.form: Beduerus — Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latinized form, Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136)

kin.label: Old French / English
kin.form: Bedivers, Bedoier — the romance forms from which Malory's Sir Bedivere descends

kin.label: Proto-Celtic (proposed)
kin.form: *Betwo-rīxs, 'birch-king' — Koch's tentative derivation from Welsh bedw, 'birch trees'; a proposal, not a settled etymology

pronunciation.note: Bedwyr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: medieval Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters — w and y are vowel-letters in Welsh, but ordinary characters of the Latin alphabet, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII form to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The name's meaning is recorded as unknown; Koch's derivation from bedw, 'birch trees', is the standard proposal and remains debated.

domains.title: Knight, One-handed
domains.subtitle: The One-Handed Spearman of Arthur's War-Band
domains.lead: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc is the great companion-hero of the oldest Welsh Arthurian tradition: the warrior who never shrank from any enterprise on which [[kai|Cei]] was bound, the one-handed spearman whose single thrust made a wound equal to nine, and the one man the triads crown with a battle-diadem above the three they name. Before French romance gave Arthur his Lancelot, the Welsh tradition gave him Bedwyr.

cards.name: The Lance of Nine Wounds
cards.desc: His one strange property in Culhwch ac Olwen: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances — one arm doing the work of nine.

cards.name: The Battle-Diadem
cards.desc: The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed names Drystan, Hueil, and Cei — then adds that one was battle-diademed above all three: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc.

cards.name: Cavall the Hound
cards.desc: In the hunting of Twrch Trwyth, the greatest boar-hunt in Welsh literature, Bedwyr led Cavall — Arthur's own hound.

cards.name: The Wooden Tweezers
cards.desc: On the summit of Pumlumon he and Cei plucked the beard of Dillus the Bearded alive with wooden tweezers — for dead, the bristles would have been brittle, and no other leash could hold the hound Drudwyn.

symbols.name: The one-handed lance
symbols.meaning: A single arm doing the work of nine — prowess measured by what remains, not what is missing

symbols.name: The battle-diadem
symbols.meaning: The triad's crown above the crowned — the one name set over Drystan, Hueil, and Cei

symbols.name: Cavall, Arthur's hound
symbols.meaning: The king's own dog entrusted to his hand in the Twrch Trwyth hunt — trust made visible

symbols.name: The wooden tweezers
symbols.meaning: The impossible instrument for the impossible task — craft serving the quest on Pumlumon

symbols.name: The sword cast back to the water
symbols.meaning: In the later Malorian tradition, Bedivere is the last knight, who returns Excalibur to the lake — loyalty outliving the kingdom

mythology.lead: Bedwyr belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian tradition: the Welsh heroic material that predates Geoffrey of Monmouth and the whole romance edifice. His dossier is compact and precise — a poem's roster, a tale's three great episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes, and the one-handed man is never the lesser of the pair.

myths.tag: Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen
myths.title: The War-Band Remembered
myths.text:
The poem known from its opening line as Pa gŵr yv y porthaur? — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh: preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen, and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. In it Arthur, halted at a fortress gate by the porter Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr, recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names Arthur speaks to prove his company.

The poem is fragmentary — it breaks off mid-recitation — but its testimony matters beyond its length: it shows a Welsh Arthurian war-band whose heroes had their own deeds long before Geoffrey of Monmouth drew Arthur into Latin history, and Bedwyr is fixed in that founding generation.

myths.title: The One-Handed Spearman
myths.text:
Culhwch ac Olwen, the earliest full Arthurian prose tale, gives Bedwyr his formal introduction when Arthur calls the companions for the quest of Olwen: Arthur called Bedwyr, 'who never shrank from any enterprise upon which Kai was bound. None was equal to him in swiftness throughout this Island except Arthur and Drych Ail Kibddar. And although he was one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle. Another property he had: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.'

The great court-list earlier in the tale quietly extends the household: Amren son of Bedwyr stands among Arthur's huntsmen, and Eneuawc daughter of Bedwyr among the golden-chained maidens of the Island — the one-handed spearman with a son and daughter woven into the fabric of the court.

myths.title: The Beard of Dillus the Bearded
myths.text:
No leash in the world could hold Drudwyn, the whelp of Greid son of Eri, save one made from the beard of Dillus Farfawc — and the beard was useless unless plucked from him alive with wooden tweezers, for once dead the bristles would turn brittle. As Cei and Bedwyr sat on a beacon cairn on the summit of Pumlumon, 'in the highest wind that ever was in the world', they spied smoke that did not bend with the wind, and found the greatest robber who ever fled from Arthur scorching a wild boar at his fire.

They let him eat his fill and sleep; they shaped the wooden tweezers while he slept; Cei dug a pit beneath him, struck him into it, and together they plucked the beard clean and slew him. The leash was made and delivered to Arthur at Celli Wic — and Arthur answered with an englyn mocking Cei's deed, at which Cei's wrath was so great that the warriors of the Island could scarcely make peace between them, and Cei never again came to Arthur's aid. The episode that shows Bedwyr and Cei at their closest is the tale's own explanation of their company's end.

myths.title: The Sword of Gwrnach and the Cauldron of Diwrnach
myths.text:
For the sword of Gwrnach the Giant, from whose castle no guest had ever returned alive, Cei went in alone under a false craft — the best burnisher of swords in the world — and won Bedwyr admission by a sign: the head of his lance would leave its shaft, draw blood from the wind, and settle on its shaft again. Inside, Cei polished the giant's sword, talked him out of his scabbard, and struck off his head with his own blade; the company despoiled the castle and bore the sword to Arthur's court by the beginning of the year.

In Ireland, for the cauldron of Diwrnach Wyddel, the embassy's request was refused outright — and then Bedwyr arose and seized the cauldron and set it on the back of Hygwyd, Arthur's cauldron-bearer, while Llenlleawg Wyddel caught up Caledfwlch, and they slew Diwrnach and his company and fought their way back to the ship Prydwen, carrying the cauldron off full of Irish treasure. The two episodes are the pair's whole method: Cei's cunning at the gate, Bedwyr's hand on the prize.

myths.title: The Diadem Above the Three
myths.text:
The Welsh triads keep the tradition's compressed memory, and they name Bedwyr twice — both times beside Cei. The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed of the Island of Britain names Drystan son of Tallwch, Hueil son of Caw, and Cei son of Cynyr — and then adds: and one was battle-diademed above all three of them, and that was Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. In the tradition's own arithmetic, the one-handed man outranks the three crowned warriors it had just named.

The second naming is the triad's own joke at the war-band's expense. In the triad of the Three Powerful Swineherds, Drystan son of Tallwch kept the swine of March son of Meirchyawn while the swineherd carried a message to Essyllt — and Arthur and March and Cei and Bedwyr were there, all four, yet did not succeed in getting so much as one pigling, neither by force, nor by deception, nor by stealth. The greatest names in the Island, together, defeated by one watchful man and a herd of pigs.

myths.title: Beduerus at Soissons
myths.text:
Geoffrey of Monmouth, drawing the Welsh heroes into his Latin history of the kings of Britain (c. 1136), makes Bedwyr into Beduerus: Arthur's cupbearer and constable of Normandy, one of the two companions — with Caius the seneschal — closest to the king. In the war against the Roman emperor Lucius Tiberius, Beduerus falls in the fighting before Soissons, struck down as the British line engages, and Arthur has him carried to Bayeux in Neustria, a city his own ancestors had built, and buried there with great lamentation.

Geoffrey's account is pseudo-history, not Welsh tradition — but it fixed Bedwyr in the Latin chronicle line that Wace and Layamon would follow, and it is the hinge on which the Welsh Bedwyr turns into the Bedivere of European romance: the companion who dies in Arthur's service, far from home, mourned by the king he served.

lore.syncretism: Bedwyr's transmission is the clearest case in the Arthurian corpus of a Welsh hero passing whole into the continental tradition: Welsh Bedwyr becomes Geoffrey's Latin Beduerus, then the Bedivers and Bedoier of Old French romance, and at last Malory's Sir Bedivere — one continuous name-line from the Black Book of Carmarthen to Caxton's print shop. Within Celtic comparison the one-handed warrior who loses nothing of his worth has tempted scholars toward the Irish parallel of [[nuada|Nuadu]] of the Silver Hand, the king who lost his arm at Mag Tuired and ruled again by means of a silver one; the handbooks treat this as a shared Celtic motif of the maimed-but-undiminished champion, not a derivation of one figure from the other. What the Welsh tradition keeps distinct is the pairing: Cei and Bedwyr are a fixed couple — the tradition names them in that order, never the reverse — as elemental a bond in early Welsh Arthurian lore as any kinship.
lore.culturalLegacy: Bedwyr's afterlife runs under a French name. Wace's Roman de Brut and Layamon's Brut carried Geoffrey's Beduerus into the vernacular chronicles; the French romances made him Bedivere, one of the first and last of the Round Table; and Malory gave him the role the whole world now knows — the last knight alive with Arthur after the day of destiny, commanded to cast Excalibur into the water, twice hiding it for its worth and twice rebuked, until at the third throw an arm clothed in white samite rose from the lake, caught the sword, brandished it thrice, and vanished. Tennyson's Idylls of the King sealed the image: it is to Bedivere that the dying Arthur speaks the great consolation — 'The old order changeth, yielding place to new' — before the barge bears him away. Twentieth-century scholarship brought the Welsh original back into view: Bromwich's edition of the triads restored the battle-diadem to Bedwyr son of Bedrawc, and the standard handbooks now present the romance Bedivere as what he is — a Welsh heroic companion who had served Arthur in Welsh for perhaps three hundred years before French poetry ever heard of him. In Wales itself the name never left: Bedwyr remains a living Welsh given name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Bedwyr is the tradition's proof that loss is not the measure of a man. The texts hand him to us already one-handed — the wound is never narrated, never mourned, never explained — and then spend every remaining line insisting on the arithmetic of what is left: one arm that sheds blood faster than three warriors, one lance that wounds like nine, one diadem above the three crowned. The silence about the missing hand is the point: the Welsh tradition does not tell a story about a maimed warrior; it tells stories about the swiftest, surest companion Arthur has, who happens to fight with one arm.

And beneath the arithmetic stands the quieter fact: he never shrank from any enterprise on which Cei was bound. The tradition could have made him Arthur's mirror or Cei's rival; it made him Cei's shadow instead — the second name in every pair, the hand on the cauldron while the cunning works the gate. Loyalty, in the oldest Welsh telling, is not obedience to the crown but fidelity to a companion: the willingness to sit in the highest wind in the world, on a cairn on Pumlumon, because that is where the quest requires the two of you to sit.
lore.originalScriptNote: Medieval Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet, and the manuscripts write the name Bedwyr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; Welsh w and y are vowel-letters, but ordinary Latin characters. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: bedwyr.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Bedwyr is a textual hero: no inscription names him, and Welsh tradition offers no relic or shrine. His manuscript witnesses are exact. The poem Pa gŵr? survives uniquely in the Black Book of Carmarthen (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 1), copied in the mid-thirteenth century and the oldest surviving manuscript wholly in Welsh. Culhwch ac Olwen survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and, in a fuller recension, in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, late fourteenth century), which also carries the great collection of the triads. The one landscape witness is genuine: Pumlumon (Plynlimon) in Ceredigion, the mountain whose summit cairns the tale makes the lookout of Cei and Bedwyr in the Dillus episode, is a real massif of the Cambrian Mountains crowned with prehistoric cairns. Geoffrey of Monmouth's burial of Beduerus at Bayeux belongs to his Norman pseudo-history, not to any Welsh memory.
